SS.L5.HIS.T01.title: Hunter-gatherers and herders in Southern Africa
SS.L5.HIS.T01.description: San hunter-gatherer society and Khoikhoi herders in the Later Stone Age; how we find out about them; rock art.
SS.L5.HIS.T01.recovery_strategy: The San and Khoikhoi were the first people of Southern Africa. The San hunted and gathered; the Khoikhoi herded livestock. They shared the land for thousands of years.

questions.question: Who were the FIRST people of Southern Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who were the first people of Southern Africa?
questions.expected: The San hunter-gatherers
questions.memo: The San (sometimes called Bushmen, though San is preferred) lived in Southern Africa for tens of thousands of years before anyone else arrived.

questions.question: What does 'hunter-gatherer' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does hunter-gatherer mean?
options: A person who hunts animals and gathers wild plants to eat
A person who works in a mine
A person who runs a shop
questions.expected: A person who hunts animals and gathers wild plants to eat
questions.memo: Hunter-gatherers don't plant or farm. They take what nature already provides — hunting animals, gathering roots, fruits, nuts and water.

questions.question: What did the SAN invent that made hunting easier?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did the San invent that made hunting more effective?
questions.expected: The bow and arrow
questions.memo: The bow and arrow let the San hunt from a distance, more safely. They also used poisons on arrow tips to bring down large animals.

questions.question: Who were the KHOIKHOI?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who were the Khoikhoi?
options: Herders who kept sheep and cattle in Southern Africa
questions.expected: Herders who kept sheep and cattle in Southern Africa
questions.memo: The Khoikhoi were closely related to the San but kept livestock — sheep first, then cattle. They moved with their animals to find good grazing.

questions.question: Which is one way we find out about the San and Khoikhoi today?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is one way we find out about the San and Khoikhoi today?
options: Rock paintings, objects they left, and stories
questions.expected: Rock paintings, objects they left, and stories
questions.memo: They didn't write — so we use what they left: rock art, tools, bones, and stories passed down through families and other communities.

questions.question: What did the San BELIEVE about sharing?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did the San believe about sharing within their group?
options: All things should be shared equally within the group
questions.expected: All things should be shared equally within the group
questions.memo: San society was deeply equal. A hunter who killed a big animal didn't keep it — it was shared with the whole group. Generosity was a core value.

questions.question: True or false: The San moved around with the SEASONS to find food.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the San moved around with the seasons to find food.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. The San knew exactly when and where different plants ripened and animals gathered. They moved with the seasons — that's how hunter-gatherers thrive.

questions.question: What is 'ROCK ART'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is rock art?
options: Paintings and engravings made on rocks and in caves long ago
questions.expected: Paintings and engravings made on rocks and in caves long ago
questions.memo: Rock art is one of humanity's oldest art forms. San rock art is found across Southern Africa and gives us a window into their lives and beliefs.

questions.question: Which animal often appears in SAN rock art?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which animal often appears in San rock art?
questions.expected: The eland
questions.memo: The eland (a large antelope) was sacred to the San and appears in many rock paintings. It was linked to their spiritual beliefs and important ceremonies.

questions.question: Where is San rock art shown on South Africa's COAT OF ARMS?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where on South Africa's coat of arms is San rock art shown?
options: The two figures greeting each other are from the Linton Rock Art Panel
It is not on the coat of arms
questions.expected: The two figures greeting each other are from the Linton Rock Art Panel
questions.memo: The figures on the coat of arms come from the Linton Panel, a famous San rock painting now kept in the Iziko Museum in Cape Town. SA honours its first people this way.

questions.question: Put these in order — a typical day for a San hunter-gatherer.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — a typical day for a San hunter-gatherer.
options: Men go out to hunt while women gather plants and water
Everyone returns and food is shared
The group sits together — stories, songs, perhaps a dance
questions.expected: Wake up at the camp,Men go out to hunt while women gather plants and water,Everyone returns and food is shared,The group sits together — stories, songs, perhaps a dance
questions.memo: Daily life was structured but free — gather what's needed, share what you find, gather around the fire. Sharing and stories held the group together.

questions.question: What did the KHOIKHOI keep that the San did NOT?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did the Khoikhoi keep that the San did not?
questions.expected: Livestock — sheep and later cattle
questions.memo: This is the main difference. Khoikhoi were PASTORALISTS — they kept animals. The San remained hunter-gatherers.

questions.question: True or false: The San used PLANTS as medicines.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the San used plants as medicines.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. The San had deep plant knowledge — what to eat, what heals which illness, which plants are poisonous. This knowledge took generations to build up.

questions.question: How did the San and Khoikhoi SHARE the land?
questions.ruby_prompt: How did the San and Khoikhoi share the same land?
options: The San used wild areas; the Khoikhoi grazed their animals in others — they could coexist
questions.expected: The San used wild areas; the Khoikhoi grazed their animals in others — they could coexist
questions.memo: Their lifestyles fit different parts of the land. Hunter-gatherers needed wildlife; herders needed grass. They lived alongside each other for many generations.

questions.question: How long ago did the LATER STONE AGE start?
questions.ruby_prompt: Roughly how long ago did the Later Stone Age start?
questions.expected: About 10 000 years ago
questions.memo: The Later Stone Age in Southern Africa goes back about 10 000 years. The San lived this way of life for most of that time.

questions.question: Why might the San have PAINTED on rocks?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do historians think the San painted on rocks?
options: To record beliefs, ceremonies, animals and events that mattered to them
Because they had nothing else to do
questions.expected: To record beliefs, ceremonies, animals and events that mattered to them
questions.memo: Many San rock paintings link to trance rituals and beliefs about the spirit world — not just pictures of daily life, but spiritual and meaningful art.

questions.question: What does 'ETHNOGRAPHY' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does ethnography mean — one of the ways we learn about the past?
options: Learning about a way of life by observing living people who still follow some of it
questions.expected: Learning about a way of life by observing living people who still follow some of it
questions.memo: Ethnography helps fill gaps. By watching modern people who still practise some hunter-gatherer ways, researchers learn what archaeology alone can't tell them.

questions.question: True or false: The San had a deep KNOWLEDGE of their environment.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the San had a deep knowledge of their environment.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. The San knew which plants gave water in dry places, which gave medicine, where animals would be in each season. Theirs was a knowledge built up over thousands of years.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing you find INTERESTING about the San.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing about the San that you find interesting.
questions.expected: I find it interesting that they shared all their food equally
questions.memo: Good answers: rock art, bow and arrow, equal sharing, plant medicine, knowing the environment, surviving for tens of thousands of years. All valid.

questions.question: Which BEST describes early Southern African society 10 000 years ago?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which best describes early Southern African society 10 000 years ago?
options: Small, mobile, deeply skilled groups who lived off and respected the land
questions.expected: Small, mobile, deeply skilled groups who lived off and respected the land
questions.memo: The first Southern Africans lived in small bands, moved with the seasons, shared what they had, and knew their land deeply. This is real and important history.

SS.L5.HIS.T02.title: The first farmers in Southern Africa
SS.L5.HIS.T02.description: Bantu-speaking farmers who entered Southern Africa 1700–2000 years ago; homesteads, crops, livestock, iron-working and pottery.
SS.L5.HIS.T02.recovery_strategy: Bantu-speaking farmers brought crops, cattle and iron-working. They lived in chiefdoms — flexible, organised societies — and shared the land with the San and Khoikhoi.

questions.question: Which group of people first brought FARMING to Southern Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who were the first people to bring farming into Southern Africa?
questions.expected: Bantu-speaking people
questions.memo: Bantu-speaking farmers moved south from central Africa about 2000 years ago, bringing crops like sorghum and the skill of working iron.

questions.question: Roughly how long ago did the first farmers reach Southern Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: Roughly how long ago did the first farmers reach Southern Africa?
questions.expected: Between 2000 and 1700 years ago
questions.memo: Archaeologists date the arrival of farmers in Southern Africa to about 2000–1700 years ago. They settled gradually across many areas.

questions.question: Which new SKILL did the Bantu-speaking farmers bring?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which important skill did the Bantu-speaking farmers bring with them?
options: Iron-working — making tools and weapons from iron
questions.expected: Iron-working — making tools and weapons from iron
questions.memo: Iron tools are stronger and longer-lasting than stone or wood. Iron-working changed farming, fighting and trade across Southern Africa.

questions.question: Which CROP did the first farmers grow?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which crop did the first farmers grow?
questions.expected: Sorghum and millet (early grains)
questions.memo: Sorghum and millet were the first staple grains — well-suited to African climates and able to survive dry spells.

questions.question: What ANIMAL was most important to the early farmers?
questions.ruby_prompt: What animal was most important to the early Bantu-speaking farmers?
questions.expected: Cattle
questions.memo: Cattle were everything — food, wealth, status and a sign of being settled. A family's cattle herd was a measure of their place in society.

questions.question: What is a 'CHIEFDOM'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a chiefdom?
options: A group of people led by a chief, with shared rules and ways of living
questions.expected: A group of people led by a chief, with shared rules and ways of living
questions.memo: Chiefdoms were political groups led by a chief. They were FLEXIBLE — people could move and join different chiefdoms. They were not 'tribes' (a word historians avoid).

questions.question: True or false: Bantu-speaking farmers WIPED OUT the San when they arrived.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the Bantu-speaking farmers wiped out the San when they arrived.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. They shared the landscape for centuries — sometimes peacefully, sometimes intermarrying. The clicks in isiZulu, isiXhosa and other Nguni languages came from Khoisan languages.

questions.question: Why is the term 'TRIBE' avoided by historians?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do historians avoid using the word tribe for African societies?
options: It wrongly suggests these societies were stuck and unchanging — they were actually flexible and changing
It means something different in maths
It is offensive in all situations
questions.expected: It wrongly suggests these societies were stuck and unchanging — they were actually flexible and changing
questions.memo: Iron Age societies were highly flexible — people moved between groups, leaders rose and fell, political power shifted. 'Tribe' freezes that into a stereotype, so historians use 'chiefdom'.

questions.question: What is a 'HOMESTEAD'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a homestead?
options: A small settlement where a family lived — huts, cattle kraal, fields
questions.expected: A small settlement where a family lived — huts, cattle kraal, fields
questions.memo: Homesteads had family huts, a kraal (enclosure) for cattle, grain storage, and fields nearby. Larger homesteads belonged to chiefs.

questions.question: Who did the IRON-WORKING in early farming societies?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who did the iron-working in early farming societies?
options: Men — it was their specialist craft
questions.expected: Men — it was their specialist craft
questions.memo: Iron-working was men's work — finding ore, building a smelter, controlling the fire, hammering hot iron into tools. Skilled smiths were highly respected.

questions.question: Who did the POTTERY-making in early farming societies?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who made the pottery in early farming societies?
options: Women — pottery was their specialist craft
questions.expected: Women — pottery was their specialist craft
questions.memo: Women made pottery — pots for cooking, water, storage, beer-making and ceremonies. Beautiful styles of pottery varied between groups.

questions.question: What are the LYDENBURG HEADS?
questions.ruby_prompt: What are the Lydenburg Heads?
options: Beautiful pottery heads from early farming societies in South Africa
questions.expected: Beautiful pottery heads from early farming societies in South Africa
questions.memo: The Lydenburg Heads are 1500-year-old clay heads found in Mpumalanga — likely used in ceremonies. They're one of the oldest known African sculptures.

questions.question: Put these in chronological order.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in chronological order — oldest first.
options: San hunter-gatherers live across Southern Africa
Bantu-speaking farmers move into Southern Africa
questions.expected: San hunter-gatherers live across Southern Africa,Khoikhoi herders begin keeping livestock,Bantu-speaking farmers move into Southern Africa,Mapungubwe kingdom rises (Grade 6 topic)
questions.memo: The big timeline: hunter-gatherers (oldest), then herders, then farmers, then kingdoms grow from those farming societies.

questions.question: What did the farmers MEAN by 'communal work parties'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What were communal work parties in early farming societies?
options: Groups of neighbours coming together to plough or harvest one family's fields
questions.expected: Groups of neighbours coming together to plough or harvest one family's fields
questions.memo: When one family's field needed work, the village turned up. Next time it would be another family. This co-operation made everyone safer.

questions.question: True or false: Children in early farming societies WORKED from a young age.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: children in early farming societies worked from a young age.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Children helped with herding, fetching water, scaring birds from crops. They contributed and learned the skills they'd need as adults.

questions.question: Why was CATTLE such an important measure of wealth?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why were cattle such an important measure of wealth in farming societies?
options: Cattle give milk, meat, hides; can be used for trade (and lobola); and they survive dry years
questions.expected: Cattle give milk, meat, hides; can be used for trade (and lobola); and they survive dry years
questions.memo: Cattle = a walking storage of value. They feed you, can be traded, and unlike maize they don't fail in one bad season — they multiply. Hence so important.

questions.question: True or false: Early farmers in Southern Africa already worked IRON before the Europeans arrived.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: early farmers in Southern Africa already worked iron long before the Europeans arrived.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Africans were making iron tools, weapons and farming implements over 1500 years BEFORE European ships reached Southern Africa. African societies were innovative on their own.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing the first farmers brought to Southern Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing the first Bantu-speaking farmers brought to Southern Africa.
questions.expected: They brought iron-working
questions.memo: Good answers: farming (crops), cattle and other livestock, iron-working, pottery, the idea of villages/homesteads, new languages. All real.

questions.question: Which Southern African LANGUAGES today come partly from Bantu speakers AND from Khoisan?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which Southern African languages today combine elements from Bantu speakers AND from Khoisan languages?
options: IsiZulu, isiXhosa and other Nguni languages — the clicks come from Khoisan
questions.expected: IsiZulu, isiXhosa and other Nguni languages — the clicks come from Khoisan
questions.memo: The clicks in isiXhosa and isiZulu (like the 'c', 'q', 'x' sounds) were borrowed from Khoisan languages — proof that these groups lived together and influenced each other.

questions.question: What does this topic teach us about African history?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the big lesson about African history from this topic?
options: Africans built innovative farming, metalworking and trading societies long before Europeans arrived
Africa was empty until Europeans came
questions.expected: Africans built innovative farming, metalworking and trading societies long before Europeans arrived
questions.memo: This is one of the most important lessons of the topic. African history is rich, ancient and innovative. The story did not start with European arrival.

SS.L5.HIS.T03.title: An ancient African society: Egypt
SS.L5.HIS.T03.description: Life in ancient Egypt — the Nile, pharaohs, pyramids, hieroglyphics, religion, medicine; Tutankhamen's tomb.
SS.L5.HIS.T03.recovery_strategy: Egypt was an early African civilisation. The Nile river made farming possible in the desert. Pharaohs ruled; pyramids were tombs; hieroglyphics were the writing.

questions.question: Which CONTINENT is Egypt on?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which continent is Egypt on?
questions.expected: Africa
questions.memo: Egypt is in the north-east of Africa. Ancient Egyptian civilisation is one of the world's oldest — and it's an AFRICAN civilisation.

questions.question: Which river made ancient Egypt possible?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which river made ancient Egypt possible?
questions.expected: The Nile
questions.memo: The Nile floods every year, bringing rich soil. Without the Nile, Egypt would be desert. Almost all ancient Egyptian life was within walking distance of the river.

questions.question: Who was a 'PHARAOH'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was a pharaoh?
options: The king (or queen) of ancient Egypt — treated as a god
questions.expected: The king (or queen) of ancient Egypt — treated as a god
questions.memo: Pharaohs were the highest rulers — political leaders AND religious figures. Their orders shaped Egypt for thousands of years.

questions.question: What were the PYRAMIDS built for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What were the Egyptian pyramids built for?
options: As tombs for pharaohs and important people
questions.expected: As tombs for pharaohs and important people
questions.memo: Pyramids were huge tombs. The Egyptians believed the pharaoh's body and soul needed to be preserved for the afterlife — hence the giant stone tombs.

questions.question: What is 'HIEROGLYPHICS'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is hieroglyphics?
options: Ancient Egyptian writing made of picture-signs
questions.expected: Ancient Egyptian writing made of picture-signs
questions.memo: Each hieroglyph stood for a sound, a syllable or a whole word. It was used for over 3000 years on temples, tombs and papyrus.

questions.question: True or false: The Egyptians believed in MANY gods.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the ancient Egyptians believed in many gods.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Egyptians had hundreds of gods — Ra (the sun), Isis (motherhood), Osiris (the afterlife), Anubis (death). Each had a role in everyday life.

questions.question: What is the SPHINX?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Sphinx?
options: A giant statue with a lion's body and a human head, built near the pyramids
questions.expected: A giant statue with a lion's body and a human head, built near the pyramids
questions.memo: The Great Sphinx at Giza is over 4500 years old and still stands today. It was likely a guardian figure for the pyramids.

questions.question: Who was TUTANKHAMEN?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Tutankhamen?
options: A young pharaoh whose tomb was found almost untouched in 1922
questions.expected: A young pharaoh whose tomb was found almost untouched in 1922
questions.memo: Tutankhamen became pharaoh as a child and died young. His tomb, discovered by Howard Carter in 1922, was filled with treasures and made him world-famous.

questions.question: Who DISCOVERED Tutankhamen's tomb?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who discovered Tutankhamen's tomb?
questions.expected: Howard Carter, a British archaeologist
questions.memo: Howard Carter searched for years before finding the tomb in 1922. His famous words upon entering: 'Wonderful things... I see wonderful things.'

questions.question: Why did the Egyptians MUMMIFY bodies?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why did the Egyptians mummify bodies?
options: They believed the body must be preserved so the soul could use it in the afterlife
They thought it would bring rain
questions.expected: They believed the body must be preserved so the soul could use it in the afterlife
questions.memo: Mummification was based on belief — preserve the body, and the spirit has a home. It involved removing organs, drying the body, and wrapping it carefully.

questions.question: Put these in order — the social structure of ancient Egypt (TOP to BOTTOM).
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order from highest to lowest in Egyptian society.
questions.expected: Pharaoh,Priests and nobles,Skilled workers and traders,Farmers and labourers
questions.memo: Pharaoh at the top, farmers at the bottom — though farmers were the biggest group and fed everyone else.

questions.question: Why was the Nile's YEARLY FLOOD so important?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why was the Nile's yearly flood so important to Egypt?
options: It left rich, dark soil on the fields — perfect for growing crops
questions.expected: It left rich, dark soil on the fields — perfect for growing crops
questions.memo: The annual flood was a gift. Egypt's whole calendar was built around it — flood season, planting season, harvest season.

questions.question: True or false: The Egyptians used MATHEMATICS and ASTRONOMY.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the Egyptians used mathematics and astronomy.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. They tracked the stars to predict the Nile flood, used geometry to build pyramids, and developed a calendar of 365 days.

questions.question: Egyptian DOCTORS were skilled at:
questions.ruby_prompt: What were Egyptian doctors skilled at?
options: Diagnosing diseases, examining patients, knowing anatomy and treating injuries
questions.expected: Diagnosing diseases, examining patients, knowing anatomy and treating injuries
questions.memo: Egyptian medicine was advanced for its time. Doctors examined patients, knew the body, made tools, and even wrote medical texts. Some of their methods are still studied today.

questions.question: What was found INSIDE Tutankhamen's tomb?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was found inside Tutankhamen's tomb?
options: Gold, jewellery, furniture and a golden mask — and his mummy
questions.expected: Gold, jewellery, furniture and a golden mask — and his mummy
questions.memo: The tomb was packed with treasures meant for the afterlife. The gold mask of Tutankhamen is now one of the most famous objects in the world.

questions.question: Why did Egyptian knowledge SPREAD to other places?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why did Egyptian knowledge spread to other places like Europe and the Middle East?
options: Through trade, travel and later conquest by other civilisations
questions.expected: Through trade, travel and later conquest by other civilisations
questions.memo: Egypt was a major centre. Traders, travellers, students and later Greek and Roman rulers carried Egyptian ideas across the Mediterranean and beyond.

questions.question: True or false: Egyptian society lasted for thousands of years.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: ancient Egyptian society lasted for thousands of years.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Egyptian civilisation lasted over 3000 years — far longer than most countries that exist today. They were stable, organised and very innovative.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing about ancient Egypt you find INTERESTING.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing about ancient Egypt that you find interesting.
questions.expected: I find the pyramids interesting because they were built so long ago
questions.memo: Good answers: pyramids, mummies, hieroglyphics, the Nile, pharaohs, gods, Tutankhamen's gold, advanced medicine. All real and valid.

questions.question: Why are PYRAMIDS still standing today?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are the Egyptian pyramids still standing thousands of years later?
options: They were built from huge stone blocks, very carefully fitted together
questions.expected: They were built from huge stone blocks, very carefully fitted together
questions.memo: Pyramids are STONE — massive, heavy blocks placed with incredible precision. Some are over 4500 years old. Egyptian engineering was remarkable.

questions.question: What does ancient Egypt teach us about AFRICAN history?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does ancient Egypt teach us about African history?
options: Africa is home to some of the world's oldest, most advanced civilisations
questions.expected: Africa is home to some of the world's oldest, most advanced civilisations
questions.memo: Egypt is part of African history. Studying it shows Africa was a place of early science, art, architecture and government long before Europe was.

SS.L5.HIS.T04.title: A heritage trail through the provinces of South Africa
SS.L5.HIS.T04.description: Examples of heritage from each of the nine provinces — sites, objects, achievements, names, architecture, art and indigenous knowledge.
SS.L5.HIS.T04.recovery_strategy: Heritage is what we inherit from the past — sites, objects, achievements, names, languages, stories, knowledge. Every province has examples that belong to all South Africans.

questions.question: What does 'HERITAGE' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does heritage mean?
options: Things from the past that we inherit and value — both physical and cultural
questions.expected: Things from the past that we inherit and value — both physical and cultural
questions.memo: Heritage can be TANGIBLE (something you can touch — a building, an object) or INTANGIBLE (a story, a song, a language, a tradition).

questions.question: How many PROVINCES does South Africa have?
questions.ruby_prompt: How many provinces does South Africa have?
questions.expected: Nine
questions.memo: Nine: Gauteng, Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape, Western Cape, Northern Cape, and North West.

questions.question: What is the 'CRADLE OF HUMANKIND'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Cradle of Humankind?
options: A World Heritage Site in Gauteng with fossils of early humans
questions.expected: A World Heritage Site in Gauteng with fossils of early humans
questions.memo: The Cradle of Humankind has some of the oldest human-related fossils ever found. It's evidence that humanity itself began in Africa.

questions.question: Where was the famous GOLDEN RHINOCEROS found?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where was the famous Golden Rhinoceros found?
questions.expected: Mapungubwe, in Limpopo Province
questions.memo: The Mapungubwe golden rhino was a royal object — a symbol of the kingdom's power. It's part of South Africa's heritage and now displayed in a special collection.

questions.question: What is the 'CASTLE OF GOOD HOPE'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Castle of Good Hope?
options: A 350-year-old Dutch fort in Cape Town — South Africa's oldest building
questions.expected: A 350-year-old Dutch fort in Cape Town — South Africa's oldest building
questions.memo: Built by the Dutch in the 1660s. It tells a complex story — Dutch colonisation, conflict with Khoikhoi, slavery, and the changing identity of Cape Town over centuries.

questions.question: Where is the famous SAN ROCK ART found in KwaZulu-Natal?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where in KwaZulu-Natal is famous San rock art found?
questions.expected: In the uKhahlamba-Drakensberg mountains
questions.memo: The Drakensberg has thousands of San rock paintings — one of the largest collections in the world. It's also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: What kind of heritage are the MAKHONJWA MOUNTAINS in Mpumalanga?
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of heritage are the Makhonjwa Mountains in Mpumalanga?
options: NATURAL heritage — they are some of the oldest mountains on Earth
questions.expected: NATURAL heritage — they are some of the oldest mountains on Earth
questions.memo: The Makhonjwa range is over 3.5 BILLION years old. Heritage isn't only human-made — natural features count too.

questions.question: What is the ALOE PLANT often used for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the aloe plant often used for in indigenous medicine?
options: Healing burns, cuts and skin problems
questions.expected: Healing burns, cuts and skin problems
questions.memo: Aloe is a traditional South African medicine. The thick gel inside the leaves soothes the skin. Many cosmetics and creams now use it.

questions.question: Who was FRANCES BAARD?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Frances Baard?
options: A South African anti-apartheid leader from the Northern Cape
questions.expected: A South African anti-apartheid leader from the Northern Cape
questions.memo: Frances Baard was a trade unionist and freedom fighter who spoke out against apartheid. The Frances Baard District in Northern Cape is named for her.

questions.question: What was KADITSHWENE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was Kaditshwene?
options: A large stone-walled town in North West province, home to thousands of people centuries ago
questions.expected: A large stone-walled town in North West province, home to thousands of people centuries ago
questions.memo: Kaditshwene was one of the largest pre-colonial towns in Southern Africa — over 20 000 people lived there. The stone walls are heritage architecture.

questions.question: True or false: Heritage can be a SONG or a story (not just an object).
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: heritage can be a song or a story — not just an object.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. INTANGIBLE heritage is just as real — songs, languages, stories, recipes, ceremonies. All carry our past into the present.

questions.question: What is 'INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is indigenous knowledge?
options: Knowledge built up by local communities over many generations
questions.expected: Knowledge built up by local communities over many generations
questions.memo: Indigenous knowledge covers traditional farming, medicine, weather signs, water finding, foods and more. Often passed down by speaking, not writing.

questions.question: Why are PROVINCIAL HERITAGE places important for ALL South Africans?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are heritage places in each province important for all South Africans?
options: They belong to the country's shared story — every province adds something
Only people from that province should care
questions.expected: They belong to the country's shared story — every province adds something
questions.memo: South African heritage is a quilt — each province sews in a square. Together they make the picture of who we are.

questions.question: Put these heritage examples with their PROVINCE.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order to match Cradle of Humankind → Mapungubwe gold → Castle of Good Hope → Drakensberg rock art.
questions.expected: Cradle of Humankind (Gauteng),Mapungubwe gold (Limpopo),Castle of Good Hope (Western Cape),Drakensberg rock art (KwaZulu-Natal)
questions.memo: Each in a different province. Together they show how varied SA's heritage is — fossils, gold, colonial fort, ancient art.

questions.question: Why might place NAMES be heritage?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are place names a form of heritage?
options: They carry meaning, history and language from earlier people
questions.expected: They carry meaning, history and language from earlier people
questions.memo: Names like uMzimkhulu (great house) or Mqhekezweni (rocky place) carry old languages and stories. When a name changes, a piece of heritage shifts.

questions.question: True or false: HERITAGE can be tangible (touchable) OR intangible (not touchable).
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: heritage can be tangible (touchable) OR intangible (not touchable).
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Tangible = the gold rhino, an old building, a stone tool. Intangible = isiZulu language, the story of Shaka, a praise poem, a recipe.

questions.question: Why might we PROTECT heritage sites?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important to protect heritage sites?
options: Once destroyed, they cannot be recovered — and they teach future generations
There is no need to protect them
questions.expected: Once destroyed, they cannot be recovered — and they teach future generations
questions.memo: A bulldozed rock painting is gone forever. A burned old building can't be rebuilt the same. Heritage protection is a gift to people not yet born.

questions.question: Tell me ONE example of heritage in YOUR province or area.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one example of heritage in your province or area.
questions.expected: Robben Island in the Western Cape
questions.memo: Good answers: any local heritage — a building, a place, a story, a person's legacy, an artwork, a tradition. All count.

questions.question: Which is a NATIONAL heritage day in South Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which day is Heritage Day in South Africa?
questions.expected: 24 September
questions.memo: Heritage Day, 24 September. South Africans celebrate the cultures, languages, foods and traditions that make the country one of the most diverse in the world.

questions.question: What does this topic teach about SOUTH AFRICAN identity?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does this topic teach us about South African identity?
options: South Africa is many cultures and stories woven into one shared country
questions.expected: South Africa is many cultures and stories woven into one shared country
questions.memo: Every province, every culture, every story contributes. That's why we sometimes call South Africa the 'rainbow nation' — many colours, one country.

SS.L5.GEO.T02.title: Physical features of South Africa
SS.L5.GEO.T02.description: South Africa's landscape — coastal plain, escarpment, plateau; main mountains, rivers and famous features; how human activity changes landscapes.
SS.L5.GEO.T02.recovery_strategy: South Africa is HIGH in the middle (a flat-topped plateau) and LOW at the coast. Rivers flow from high places down to the sea. The Drakensberg is the highest range.

questions.question: What is a 'PLATEAU'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a plateau?
options: A large area of high, flat land
questions.expected: A large area of high, flat land
questions.memo: The middle of South Africa is a plateau — high in the air but flat on top. The Highveld is part of this plateau.

questions.question: What is an 'ESCARPMENT'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is an escarpment?
options: A long steep edge where high land drops down to lower land
questions.expected: A long steep edge where high land drops down to lower land
questions.memo: South Africa's Great Escarpment runs around much of the country — separating the high plateau from the lower coastal plain.

questions.question: What is the 'COASTAL PLAIN'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the coastal plain?
options: The low, flat land along the coast (between the sea and the escarpment)
Land in the middle of the country
questions.expected: The low, flat land along the coast (between the sea and the escarpment)
questions.memo: Coastal plain = the strip of low land near the sea. Durban, East London and Cape Town are all on or near the coastal plain.

questions.question: Which is SOUTH AFRICA's highest mountain range?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is South Africa's highest mountain range?
questions.expected: The Drakensberg (uKhahlamba)
questions.memo: The Drakensberg has the highest peaks in Southern Africa — Thabana Ntlenyana (in Lesotho) is over 3 400m above sea level.

questions.question: Which famous mountain is in CAPE TOWN?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which famous mountain is in Cape Town?
questions.expected: Table Mountain
questions.memo: Table Mountain has a flat top that looks like a table. It's part of the Cape Floral Region and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: Where do most rivers in South Africa BEGIN?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where do most South African rivers begin?
options: In the high mountains and plateau
questions.expected: In the high mountains and plateau
questions.memo: Rivers always flow from HIGH to LOW. They start in high ground where rain falls or snow melts, then flow downhill to the sea.

questions.question: What is a 'TRIBUTARY'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a tributary?
options: A smaller river that joins a bigger river
questions.expected: A smaller river that joins a bigger river
questions.memo: Like branches of a tree feeding the trunk. The Gariep (Orange) river has many tributaries that feed water into it from far around.

questions.question: What is the BIGGEST river in South Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is South Africa's biggest (longest) river?
questions.expected: The Gariep (Orange) River
questions.memo: The Gariep flows from the Drakensberg in Lesotho all the way to the Atlantic at the Namibian border — about 2 200 km.

questions.question: What is a 'CATCHMENT AREA' of a river?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a river's catchment area?
options: All the land where rain that falls eventually flows into that river
The mouth of the river only
Only the city near the river
questions.expected: All the land where rain that falls eventually flows into that river
questions.memo: Every river has a catchment — the area where rain flows into it. Damage in the catchment (pollution, deforestation) affects the river.

questions.question: What is the 'KAROO'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Karoo?
options: A large, dry, mostly flat region in central South Africa
questions.expected: A large, dry, mostly flat region in central South Africa
questions.memo: The Great Karoo and Little Karoo together cover huge areas. Very dry, sparse plants, sheep farms, fascinating fossils. A unique South African landscape.

questions.question: What is the 'HIGHVELD'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Highveld?
options: A high, mostly flat grassland area in central South Africa (Gauteng, Free State)
questions.expected: A high, mostly flat grassland area in central South Africa (Gauteng, Free State)
questions.memo: Highveld = high field. Cold winters, hot wet summers, big skies, lots of grass. Most of SA's gold mines are on the Highveld.

questions.question: What is the 'LOWVELD'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Lowveld?
options: A lower, hotter region in eastern South Africa — includes Kruger National Park
questions.expected: A lower, hotter region in eastern South Africa — includes Kruger National Park
questions.memo: Lowveld = low ground east of the escarpment. Hotter and more humid than the Highveld. The Kruger and Mpumalanga's wildlife areas are here.

questions.question: What is AUGRABIES FALLS?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is Augrabies Falls?
options: A famous waterfall on the Gariep River in the Northern Cape
questions.expected: A famous waterfall on the Gariep River in the Northern Cape
questions.memo: Augrabies is one of South Africa's most dramatic waterfalls — when the Gariep is full, water thunders down the gorge.

questions.question: Put these in order — a river's JOURNEY.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — a river's journey from start to sea.
options: Small streams form and join into bigger rivers
The river flows across the land
The river reaches the sea at the coast
questions.expected: Rain falls in high mountains,Small streams form and join into bigger rivers,The river flows across the land,The river reaches the sea at the coast
questions.memo: Every river follows this path. Understand this and you understand how water shapes the land.

questions.question: How can BUILDING A DAM change the physical environment?
questions.ruby_prompt: How can building a dam change the physical environment?
options: It floods the area behind the wall, changing the river and what lives nearby
It moves the river to the sea
questions.expected: It floods the area behind the wall, changing the river and what lives nearby
questions.memo: Dams create huge man-made lakes. This drowns trees, displaces wildlife, sometimes displaces people. Dams help (water, electricity) but also change a landscape forever.

questions.question: How does ROAD BUILDING change the landscape?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does road building change the natural landscape?
options: It cuts through hills, fills valleys, drains wetlands and removes vegetation
questions.expected: It cuts through hills, fills valleys, drains wetlands and removes vegetation
questions.memo: Roads need flat surfaces. So engineers cut into hills, fill in low spots, and clear plants. This is necessary but it does change the land permanently.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa has a COAST on both the Atlantic AND Indian Ocean.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa has a coast on both the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. The west coast is the cold Atlantic; the east coast is the warm Indian Ocean. The two meet near Cape Agulhas — the southern tip of Africa.

questions.question: What is a CAPE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a cape (in geography)?
options: A piece of land that sticks out into the sea
questions.expected: A piece of land that sticks out into the sea
questions.memo: Cape Point and Cape Agulhas are famous SA capes. The Cape province got its name from these points of land sticking into the sea.

questions.question: Tell me ONE physical feature near where you live.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one physical feature near where you live — a river, hill, mountain, valley, anything.
questions.expected: The Jukskei river flows near my home
questions.memo: Good answers: a river, hill, mountain, valley, coast, koppie, beach, gorge. Any real feature of the local landscape.

questions.question: Why do most South African CITIES lie on the COAST or on RIVERS?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are most major South African cities on the coast or near rivers?
options: People settled near water — for drinking, farming, fishing and trade
questions.expected: People settled near water — for drinking, farming, fishing and trade
questions.memo: Water is life. Cape Town, Durban, East London, Port Elizabeth are coastal. Joburg is unusual — built around GOLD, not water (which is why it imports water from far away).

SS.L5.GEO.T03.title: Weather, climate and vegetation of South Africa
SS.L5.GEO.T03.description: Elements of weather; difference between weather and climate; rainfall patterns; natural vegetation including savannah grasslands.
SS.L5.GEO.T03.recovery_strategy: Weather = TODAY. Climate = the PATTERN over many years. Natural vegetation is plants that grow on their own, shaped by climate. Different climates grow different plants.

questions.question: What is the difference between WEATHER and CLIMATE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather is what's happening today; climate is the pattern over many years
They mean exactly the same thing
Weather is hot; climate is cold
Climate only happens at the coast
questions.expected: Weather is what's happening today; climate is the pattern over many years
questions.memo: Weather changes day to day — rain today, sun tomorrow. Climate is the long-run pattern of a place, built up over many years.

questions.question: Which is an ELEMENT of weather?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is an element of weather?
options: Temperature, wind, cloud cover and rainfall
questions.expected: Temperature, wind, cloud cover and rainfall
questions.memo: Weather has several parts — how hot/cold (temperature), how windy, how cloudy, and how much rain. All four together describe the weather.

questions.question: What is 'PRECIPITATION'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does precipitation mean?
options: Water that falls from the sky — rain, hail or snow
questions.expected: Water that falls from the sky — rain, hail or snow
questions.memo: Precipitation = any water falling from clouds. Most of SA gets rain; high mountains get snow in winter; some places get hail with summer storms.

questions.question: What instrument measures TEMPERATURE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What instrument measures temperature?
questions.expected: A thermometer
questions.memo: Thermometers measure how hot or cold the air is — usually in degrees Celsius in South Africa.

questions.question: What instrument measures RAINFALL?
questions.ruby_prompt: What instrument measures rainfall?
questions.expected: A rain gauge
questions.memo: A rain gauge collects rain. You can read off the depth in millimetres. A simple jar with a ruler works as a homemade rain gauge.

questions.question: What does a WIND SOCK or WIND VANE show?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a wind sock or wind vane show you?
options: The direction the wind is blowing from
questions.expected: The direction the wind is blowing from
questions.memo: Wind direction matters — for weather forecasts, for pilots, for sailors. We name a wind by where it comes FROM (a 'south-east wind' blows from the south-east).

questions.question: Most of South Africa gets its rain in:
questions.ruby_prompt: Most of South Africa gets its rain in which season?
questions.expected: Summer (October to March)
questions.memo: Most of SA is a SUMMER rainfall area. Big thunderstorms come in summer afternoons. The Western Cape is the main exception — see the next question.

questions.question: Which part of South Africa gets WINTER rainfall?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which part of South Africa gets most of its rain in winter?
questions.expected: The Western Cape (around Cape Town)
questions.memo: Cape Town has a winter rainfall climate — like the Mediterranean. Hot dry summers and wet cool winters. The fynbos plants of the Cape evolved for this.

questions.question: What is 'NATURAL VEGETATION'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is natural vegetation?
options: Plants that grow on their own in an area, without being planted by humans
questions.expected: Plants that grow on their own in an area, without being planted by humans
questions.memo: Natural vegetation is what GROWS THERE BY ITSELF — shaped by climate, soil and water. Different climates = different vegetation.

questions.question: What is a 'SAVANNAH'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a savannah?
options: A warm grassland with scattered trees — like the bushveld and Kruger area
questions.expected: A warm grassland with scattered trees — like the bushveld and Kruger area
questions.memo: Savannah = grass with trees here and there. Found in warm areas with a wet summer and dry winter. Home to many of Africa's famous animals.

questions.question: Why do most savannah trees have SMALL or NEEDLE-LIKE leaves?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do many savannah trees have small or needle-like leaves?
options: Small leaves lose less water — useful in a dry climate
Small leaves are easier to draw
questions.expected: Small leaves lose less water — useful in a dry climate
questions.memo: Plants adapt to climate. Big leaves lose lots of water; small or needle leaves lose less. Acacia and karoo plants show this beautifully.

questions.question: True or false: Climate affects what kind of CLOTHES people wear.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: climate affects what clothes people wear.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. In hot climates, light and loose clothes; in cold climates, warm layers. Daily life everywhere is shaped by climate.

questions.question: Why is the Western Cape called a 'MEDITERRANEAN' climate?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is the Western Cape called a Mediterranean climate?
options: Hot dry summers and cool wet winters — same as the Mediterranean coast of Europe
questions.expected: Hot dry summers and cool wet winters — same as the Mediterranean coast of Europe
questions.memo: Same climate, half a world apart. That's why grapes, olives and wheat (Mediterranean plants) grow so well in the Cape.

questions.question: Why is GAUTENG often hot in summer with afternoon thunderstorms?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does Gauteng often have hot summers with afternoon thunderstorms?
options: The hot air rises during the day, cools and forms clouds and storms by afternoon
questions.expected: The hot air rises during the day, cools and forms clouds and storms by afternoon
questions.memo: Highveld summers = sunny mornings, building clouds by lunch, thunderstorms by 3–4pm. A real pattern. The sun's heating drives the daily cycle.

questions.question: Put these in order from WETTEST to DRIEST in South Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order from wettest to driest in South Africa.
questions.expected: KwaZulu-Natal coast (very wet),Gauteng (summer rains),Karoo (dry, some rain),Northern Cape / Namib edge (very dry)
questions.memo: SA dries out as you move from east to west. The Indian Ocean side gets wet air; the Atlantic side gets dry air.

questions.question: How does CLIMATE affect what FARMERS can grow?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does climate affect what farmers can grow?
options: Different climates suit different crops — maize needs summer rain, wheat needs winter rain
questions.expected: Different climates suit different crops — maize needs summer rain, wheat needs winter rain
questions.memo: Wheat in the Western Cape (winter rain), maize on the Highveld (summer rain), sugar cane in KZN (warm and wet). The map of farming follows the climate map.

questions.question: True or false: ANIMALS in the savannah are linked to the natural vegetation.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: animals in a savannah are linked to the natural vegetation.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Zebra and wildebeest eat grass; giraffes eat tree leaves; lions eat the grass-eaters. Take away the plants — the animal world falls apart.

questions.question: Why do FARMERS WATCH the weather forecast?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do farmers watch the weather forecast carefully?
options: Weather decides when to plant, when to harvest, when to protect animals from cold or storms
Weather has no effect on farming
Only city people watch the weather
questions.expected: Weather decides when to plant, when to harvest, when to protect animals from cold or storms
questions.memo: A wrong-timed planting can lose a crop. A frost can kill lambs. Farmers and weather forecasters are old partners.

questions.question: Tell me what the WEATHER is like where you live in WINTER.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me what the weather is like where you live in winter.
questions.expected: Where I live the winters are cold and dry with frost in the mornings
questions.memo: Good answers describe real local conditions — cold, dry, frosty (Gauteng); cool and rainy (Cape Town); warm but dry (KZN coast); mild (Durban). All real.

questions.question: Which BEST describes South Africa's climate overall?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which best describes South Africa's climate overall?
options: Varied — different climates in different regions, mostly warm and dry
questions.expected: Varied — different climates in different regions, mostly warm and dry
questions.memo: SA's climate varies a lot — coastal vs inland, summer rain vs winter rain, hot Lowveld vs cool Highveld. This variety is part of what makes the country so rich.

SS.L5.GEO.T04.title: Minerals and mining in South Africa
SS.L5.GEO.T04.description: SA's main minerals (gold, platinum, diamonds, iron ore, coal); ways of mining; environmental impact; health and safety of miners.
SS.L5.GEO.T04.recovery_strategy: Minerals are non-renewable — once mined, they're gone. SA is famous for gold, platinum and diamonds. Mining brings wealth but can hurt land, air, water and miners' health.

questions.question: What is a 'MINERAL'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a mineral?
options: A natural substance found in the earth — like gold, iron or diamond
questions.expected: A natural substance found in the earth — like gold, iron or diamond
questions.memo: Minerals come from rocks in the earth. Some are very valuable (gold, platinum, diamonds); others are useful in big quantities (iron, coal).

questions.question: What does 'NON-RENEWABLE' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does non-renewable mean?
options: Once used up, it cannot grow back — it is gone forever
It is a type of plant
questions.expected: Once used up, it cannot grow back — it is gone forever
questions.memo: Minerals took millions of years to form. Once mined and used, we cannot make new ones. That's why we use them carefully.

questions.question: Which mineral is South Africa MOST famous for?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which mineral is South Africa most famous for?
questions.expected: Gold
questions.memo: South Africa was the world's biggest gold producer for many decades. Johannesburg ('eGoli — place of gold') was built on it.

questions.question: Which is ANOTHER very important South African mineral?
questions.ruby_prompt: Besides gold, which other mineral is South Africa world-famous for?
questions.expected: Platinum
questions.memo: South Africa has most of the world's platinum. Used in car parts, jewellery, electronics and medical equipment.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa mines DIAMONDS.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa mines diamonds.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Kimberley is famous for diamond mining. The Big Hole there was dug entirely by hand — one of the largest hand-dug holes in the world.

questions.question: What is COAL used for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is coal used for?
options: To generate electricity and make steel
questions.expected: To generate electricity and make steel
questions.memo: Most of SA's electricity comes from coal-fired power stations. Coal also helps make steel. But burning coal pollutes the air, so the world is moving away from it.

questions.question: Is COAL technically a 'MINERAL'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Is coal technically a mineral?
options: No — it is formed from old plant remains, but we still mine it like a mineral
Yes, exactly the same as a mineral
questions.expected: No — it is formed from old plant remains, but we still mine it like a mineral
questions.memo: Coal formed from ancient plants buried millions of years ago. Scientists call it a fossil fuel, not a mineral — but we mine and treat it like a mineral.

questions.question: What is OPEN-PIT mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is open-pit mining?
options: Digging a huge hole from the surface to reach minerals near the top of the ground
questions.expected: Digging a huge hole from the surface to reach minerals near the top of the ground
questions.memo: If the mineral is near the surface, open-pit mining is cheaper and faster. The Big Hole in Kimberley and Palabora copper mine are examples.

questions.question: What is DEEP-LEVEL (shaft) mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is deep-level shaft mining?
options: Digging deep shafts and tunnels underground to reach minerals far below the surface
questions.expected: Digging deep shafts and tunnels underground to reach minerals far below the surface
questions.memo: South Africa has some of the deepest mines in the world — some go DOWN over 3km. Gold and platinum are mined this way.

questions.question: What is the BIG environmental problem with mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a big environmental problem with mining?
options: It pollutes water and air, destroys vegetation, and leaves big waste piles
questions.expected: It pollutes water and air, destroys vegetation, and leaves big waste piles
questions.memo: Mining changes land permanently. Dust gets into the air, chemicals into water, plants and animals lose habitat. Modern mining tries to limit these effects.

questions.question: What is SILICOSIS?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is silicosis — a disease miners can get?
options: A lung disease from breathing in dust over many years underground
questions.expected: A lung disease from breathing in dust over many years underground
questions.memo: Underground rock dust hurts the lungs. Many South African miners have silicosis from years working in deep mines. Mines now MUST control dust.

questions.question: Why is it HOT deep underground?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it so hot deep underground in a mine?
options: The earth gets hotter the deeper you go
questions.expected: The earth gets hotter the deeper you go
questions.memo: The deeper the mine, the hotter the rocks. SA's deep gold mines reach over 50°C without cooling. Big fans and ice are used to make it survivable.

questions.question: Which is a RULE that protects miners?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a safety rule that protects miners?
options: Wearing helmets, masks and boots; following safety procedures; regular inspections
questions.expected: Wearing helmets, masks and boots; following safety procedures; regular inspections
questions.memo: Mining is dangerous. Safety equipment, training, ventilation and inspections save lives. Workers also have unions to push for better conditions.

questions.question: Why does South Africa MINE in the first place?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does South Africa mine so much?
options: The country has rich mineral deposits, and mining earns big income and many jobs
questions.expected: The country has rich mineral deposits, and mining earns big income and many jobs
questions.memo: Mining built modern SA. It earns export money, employs hundreds of thousands of people, and supports many other industries.

questions.question: Put these in order — what happens to a piece of GOLD from underground to a shop.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — what happens to gold from underground to a jewellery shop.
options: Miners dig up the gold-bearing rock deep underground
Rock is brought to the surface and crushed
Gold is separated from the rock and melted into bars
Bars are sold and made into jewellery or kept as wealth
questions.expected: Miners dig up the gold-bearing rock deep underground,Rock is brought to the surface and crushed,Gold is separated from the rock and melted into bars,Bars are sold and made into jewellery or kept as wealth
questions.memo: Mine → crush → separate → melt → trade. A long, expensive process. That's part of why gold is so valuable.

questions.question: What is IRON ORE used for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is iron ore used for?
options: Making steel — used in buildings, cars, ships, machines
questions.expected: Making steel — used in buildings, cars, ships, machines
questions.memo: Iron ore is the start of most steel. Steel is in almost everything modern — bridges, cars, fridges, knives. SA has big iron ore mines like Sishen.

questions.question: True or false: All of South Africa's MINERAL wealth will last forever.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa's mineral wealth will last forever.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. Mines run out. As old mines close, communities must find new work. Mining areas need to plan for life AFTER mining.

questions.question: Lerato's father works in a deep gold mine. What is one DANGER he faces?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's father works in a deep gold mine. What's one danger he faces?
options: Rock falls, heat, dust, and equipment accidents
questions.expected: Rock falls, heat, dust, and equipment accidents
questions.memo: Deep mining is one of the hardest jobs in the world. Strict safety procedures save lives. Many miners support whole families with their work.

questions.question: Tell me ONE everyday item that uses a MINERAL.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one everyday item that uses a mineral.
questions.expected: My cell phone uses gold and other metals
questions.memo: Good answers: cell phone (gold, copper, rare metals), car (iron/steel, aluminium, platinum), jewellery, batteries, electric wires, money (copper coins). All real.

questions.question: What is the BIGGEST lesson about mining?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the biggest lesson about mining and the country?
options: Mining gives wealth and jobs but must balance environment, safety and the future
Mining is purely good with no problems
Mining is purely bad with no benefits
questions.expected: Mining gives wealth and jobs but must balance environment, safety and the future
questions.memo: Mining is both/and — wealth AND damage. The challenge is to mine in a way that's fair to workers, kind to the environment, and plans for the future.
